alt: A two-page quick start guide for methadone treatment, detailing dosage, regulations, patient management, and drug interactions.
summary:
This document, titled "Methadone Quick Start" by CA Bridge, serves as a comprehensive guide for healthcare providers on initiating and managing methadone treatment for Opioid Use Disorder (OUD). The first page outlines a quick start protocol for new patients, including initial dosing (Day 1: 30 mg, Day 2: 40 mg, Day 3: 50 mg, with subsequent increases), and specific instructions for hospitalized patients, such as administering additional doses if no sedation and continuing methadone throughout hospitalization. It also provides guidance for patients already in methadone treatment, including protocols for missed doses, and highlights complicating factors like low opioid tolerance, QTc prolongation, and concomitant use of sedatives. Key regulations are mentioned, such as general acute care hospitals treating addiction under existing licenses, ED administration limits, and the inability to prescribe methadone for OUD at discharge.

The legal significance of this document is underscored by its references to regulatory bodies and changes. It notes the removal of the X-waiver in January 2023, simplifying methadone administration. It also mentions that hospitals can apply to the DEA for a waiver to dispense a 72-hour supply to bridge patients to a clinic, and that Opioid Treatment Programs (OTPs) can only provide methadone to patients opioid-dependent for at least 6 months. The document is a product of CA Bridge, a program of the Public Health Institute, in collaboration with the California Department of Health Care Services, and is licensed under Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International, indicating its intended use as a public health resource.

While the document is primarily instructional, it emphasizes critical warnings regarding drug interactions. It lists medications that increase methadone metabolism (decreasing its effect and increasing opioid withdrawal risk) and those that decrease methadone metabolism (increasing sedation and CNS depression). It advises checking for drug-drug interactions before starting new medications to avoid over-sedation or withdrawal. The document itself is a guide and does not present internal discrepancies; rather, it provides clear, step-by-step instructions and warnings for safe and effective methadone management.

BRIDGE
Methadone Quick Start
Follow-up clinic (phone, address, intake hours):
Opioid use disorder (OUD) & wants methadone*
No complicating factors**
New start
In treatment
Methadone vs buprenorphine (bup) for patients*
• Methadone ED starts are only suggested when
patients are able to follow up in a methadone
clinic (OTP) within 72 hours. Work with local
clinics to expedite follow up.
Day 1: 30 mg
methadone
Call opioid treatment
program to confirm dose***
• Methadone and bup are both great options that
decrease all cause mortality and overdose.
• If a patient is struggling to wait for withdrawal to
start bup, methadone may be an option.
• You usually must go to an OTP for daily dosing.
• If methadone dose too high or if mixed with
other depressants, may cause sedation.
Hospitalized Patients
Complicating Factors**
• RR <10 or sedated
• Low opioid tolerance
Day 2: 40 mg
methadone
May administer an
additional 10 mg
methadone 4 hours
after daily dose if no
sedation.
• Allergy to methadone
• Known QTc ≥500 (do not need to check EKG to
start methadone routinely)
• Recent use of benzodiazepines, alcohol, or other
sedatives
Day 3: 50 mg
methadone
• Severe liver disease
• Medically unstable
• Day 4 and beyond: Increase methadone by 10 mg every
3-5 days.
• Methadone safe in pregnancy & breastfeeding
• If methadone doses do not control withdrawal, short acting
opioid agonists can be administered.
• Methadone can be continued throughout hospitalization. No
additional licensing required (X-waiver removed, Jan 2023).
Patients already in methadone treatment***
• Call clinic to confirm dose amount and when it
was last administered.
• If unable to confirm dose, treat as a new start
until able to confirm.
DISCHARGE
• Methadone dispensed from a clinic is never
listed in CURES, and some hospitals urine
toxicology will not show methadone.
• Provide patient with information on how to link to methadone clinic next
day, or have them return for doses every 72 hours. Methadone may not
be prescribed at discharge for the treatment of OUD.
• If 1-2 days missed, administer the full dose.
•
If additional days missed, ask the clinic for
recommended dosing. Ex: 90% if 3 days missed,
80% if 4 days missed, 70% if 5 days missed, 60%
if 6 days missed, 50% if 7 days missed, 40% if 8
days missed.
• Patient should have naloxone 4mg/0.1ml in hand at discharge.
Regulations
• General acute care hospitals may treat addiction with methadone under their existing license.
• ED may administer methadone for 3 days in a row. If a patient is hospitalized, administer throughout their hospitalization.
• Methadone cannot be prescribed for the treatment of OUD.
•
Hospitals can apply to the DEA for a waiver to dispense a 72 hour supply of methadone to help patients connect to a clinic.
• OTPs can only provide methadone if patients have been opioid dependent for at least 6 months.
Pharmacologic notes:
• Can use adjunctive medications for withdrawal symptoms.
• In cases of high tolerance, including fentanyl use, may need additional dose of full opioid agonists to control withdrawal; only while
patient is in the hospital.
• Sedation from methadone peaks at 3-4 hours after each dose, patients experiencing sedation should not receive additional doses.
• Half-life of methadone is more than 24 hours, so doses can stack and sedation can occur after multiple days at the same dose.
•
Bup should not be given to patients who are currently taking methadone, as this would cause withdrawal.
• Methadone has many significant drug-drug interactions. Before starting new medications, always check the effect on methadone
levels to avoid over-sedation or withdrawal.
